This makes the focus's handover legible as an active orientation that continues into ethical action and a path.
findings.mechanism: The focus clause joins handing over the face toward God with the circumstantial state of doing good. The near-repeated clauses in 2:112 and 4:125 preserve that relation; 4:125 adds following Abraham, while the local contrast at 31:21 distinguishes revealed direction from inherited following and 31:18 gives beneficence a bodily ethical contrast. These separate triggers meet the focus's handover, direction, and active good-doing without replacing any of them.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see surrender continuing through action: the face has a destination, and the person remains an agent of good.
findings.containment: The focus still states that whoever submits their face to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold. The wider parallels do not make the face mean only a route, turn the repeated wording into a forecast, or displace the ordinary handover reading. Remote target morphology is not supplied, so the parallels are assessed from their exact Arabic surface.

findings.claim: The focus's final outcome of all affairs can be read as the edge that follows present deeds. In 22:41, public acts are followed by the same phrase assigning the outcome of affairs to God; 65:9 links an affair with its ruinous consequence. The wider relation makes outcome carry the history of what came before it.
findings.mechanism: The focus places the outcome noun over the plural field of affairs. In 22:41, prayer, giving, and public moral action precede the repeated affairs-and-outcome phrase; in 65:9, an affair is explicitly tasted through its consequence before its outcome is named. Those sequences activate the focus's following and consequence facets, turning the coda from an unrelated terminal event into what follows an affair's course.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive an outcome as the next edge of an affair, with the preceding action still present in its consequence.
findings.containment: The focus continues to say that the final outcome of all affairs is directed to God. This does not promise an immediate visible result for every act or let a reader forecast the full outcome.

epistemic.reason: A trusted published reading and a legacy walk converge, while the supplied target Arabic supports the action-to-consequence sequence without remote morphology.

Those structures meet the focus attachment and change it from subjective reassurance into a support image, while the HFT trace's exact role remains attributed.

The comparison does not turn 31:10 into a literal explanation of the focus, promise physical protection, or deny the alternative that the creation passage generally strengthens trust. findings.title: A grip enacted through endurance
findings.claim: The focus's achieved grip can carry orientation into sustained practice under pressure. In 31:17, worship, public good, restraint from wrong, and patience under affliction lead into a resolute undertaking; 11:49 pairs patience with an eventual outcome, and 22:41 places public ethical action before the outcome of affairs.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies holding, firmness, and beneficent action. The exact HFT trace puts patience and resolve in 31:17, whose imperatives make continuation visible; 11:49 independently joins patience to outcome, while 22:41 joins public deeds to the same affairs coda. The focus grip consequently shifts from a static possession toward durable self-command and resolved continuation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the handhold as an orientation that remains active when consequences arrive, rather than a belief that ends at assent.
findings.containment: Patience and resolve are contextual roles, not lexical meanings of the handhold. The focus still states an achieved grasp; the alternative remains that 31:17 lists virtues without defining the focus metaphor, and the wider verses do not guarantee a particular worldly result.

epistemic.reason: The HFT trace supplies exact Arabic anchors and coordinates, but context roots and role assignments are attributed; wider exact Arabic supports the patience-to-outcome relation without remote morphology.

findings.title: Surrender carried through visible conduct
findings.claim: The focus joins a face directed to God with beneficent action. Wider examples of ihsan describe giving, restraining anger, and forgiving people; the surrounding 31:18–20 scenes give that conduct bodily form in cheek, gait, voice, and the visible and inward registers. Together they let the focus's surrendered face be read as an orientation carried through public behavior and inward integrity.
findings.mechanism: The focus face and good-doer supply the carriers. The attributed roles in 31:18–20 connect face-direction with bodily posture, measured movement and speech, and paired visible/inward favor. The independent 3:134 examples return through the focus muhsin condition, making beneficence a set of practices rather than only a label. The two-faced branch remains a contrast to the outer/inward alignment, not a literal reading of the singular focus word.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see surrender as something expressed in how one turns toward people, moves, speaks, and joins outward conduct to inward direction.
findings.containment: The focus word for face does not lexically mean all behavior, and its singular form is not a two-faced collocation. The outer/inward connection is a contextual resonance, with the live alternative that face simply means the whole self without special public-postural force.

epistemic.reason: The HFT trace supplies exact anchor ayahs and coordinates, but context segmentation, roots, and roles are attributed; 3:134 supplies exact Arabic without target morphology.
